paragraphs: AdLift aims to protect 3D Gaussian Splatting assets from unauthorized instruction-driven editing. Protection developed for a single image does not directly solve this problem: a 3D asset can be viewed from many directions, and a useful safeguard must interfere with editing while remaining visually imperceptible. The paper addresses these requirements by transferring tightly bounded image perturbations into a safeguard represented by 3D Gaussians.

Its optimization alternates between image space and the Gaussian representation. First, a tailored projected-gradient procedure truncates gradients flowing back from the editing model and restricts the size of changes in the rendered image. Then, image-to-Gaussian fitting transfers those changes into the safeguard parameters. Repeating this process across training views connects explicit image-level bounds with protection stored in the 3D asset itself.

The reported qualitative and quantitative evaluations show effective protection against instruction-driven image and 3DGS editing methods. Protection extends to novel views as well as training views while remaining imperceptible. These findings support the approach’s central idea: coordinating bounded perturbations through a shared 3D representation can make the safeguard useful beyond individual protected renderings.
icml-2026-adlift-lifting-adversarial-per.tldr: AdLift embeds bounded image perturbations into 3D Gaussians to provide visually imperceptible protection against instruction-driven editing across views.

paragraphs: Dynamic Structural Distillation addresses a tension in long-term forecasting: powerful Transformer teachers are computationally expensive, while lightweight linear students have limited expressive capacity. Simply training a student to reproduce each teacher prediction can also transfer the teacher’s uncertainty or mistakes. The paper therefore transfers relationships within learned representations and adjusts how strongly the student follows its teacher.

The framework first introduces LMP-Net, which expands features into a higher-dimensional latent space while retaining lightweight inference. Dual Manifold Alignment then addresses differences between token-based and point-based architectures. Similarity-preserving distillation transfers relationships among features, while optimal transport aligns their geometry. These two forms of alignment provide structural supervision beyond matching individual forecast values.

A further component adjusts distillation using a dataset-level regime prior and confidence-based gating, reducing the risk of misleading teacher guidance. Experiments on five benchmarks report improvements for lightweight students across data regimes and compatibility with different teacher architectures. The stated accuracy–efficiency trade-off suggests that richer student representations and selective structural transfer can work together without giving up the practical benefits of lightweight forecasting.
icml-2026-beyond-point-predictions-manif.tldr: Dynamic Structural Distillation improves lightweight forecasting by transferring feature structure and adaptively limiting potentially misleading teacher guidance.

paragraphs: This paper develops continuous control over an LLM’s expressed personality by steering its internal activations during inference. Conventional persona alignment can require costly data collection and separate training for different personalities. Here, the base model’s parameters stay fixed, and reusable steering vectors provide adjustable controls over multiple traits.

Combining those controls requires accounting for their interactions. The method repeatedly retrains probes on the residual stream after earlier trait interventions have modified it, making subsequent interventions compatible with previous ones. An automated pipeline chooses intervention layers by examining activation separation. It also calibrates steering strengths through hyperparameter optimization, seeking stronger personality alignment while constraining perplexity.

Once the vectors have been established, users can create new personality combinations by changing their coefficients without additional training. Evaluations use an LLM judge to assess individual trait changes and the Big Five inventory to assess the broader personality profile. The findings support modular inference-time control over both specific traits and their combined expression, with preparation concentrated in constructing and calibrating the reusable interventions.
icml-2026-controllable-and-explainable-p.tldr: Reusable activation-steering vectors let users adjust and combine LLM personality traits at inference time without changing base model parameters.

paragraphs: This paper examines why multimodal systems can preserve average performance yet remain unreliable on adverse cases when sensors drop out or degrade. Its comparison holds observable support fixed: the failures occur over the same observable possibilities, even between runs with matched averages. The explanation separates seeing relevant environments from adequately updating the parameters responsible for handling them.

Gated routing directs information through different parameter groups. Some groups can strongly influence tail outcomes while receiving relatively few updates, despite complete environment coverage. Tail-focused evaluation then magnifies their errors. The authors introduce TailPressure, a statistic derived from gating logs that measures tail-relevant interaction relative to parameter exposure, making this mismatch auditable.

Their H-CES controller stabilizes pressure across groups using deterministic increment-branch gating and independently managed group-wise weight decay. It leaves the loss and inference procedure unchanged. Across the reported multimodal settings and backbones, it improves reliability on same-support tails while preserving clean performance. The findings identify training exposure as a practical control point when average accuracy and environment coverage alone conceal uneven reliability.
icml-2026-coverage-not-exposure-auditabl.tldr: H-CES improves multimodal tail reliability by auditing and stabilizing parameter-group exposure that average performance and environment coverage can conceal.

paragraphs: WiCAT studies how to learn shared representations from widefield calcium imaging collected across multiple subjects. These recordings capture cortical dynamics but contain high-dimensional spatial and temporal structure alongside substantial activity unrelated to the task. Such complexity has largely confined modeling to individual sessions, limiting the ability to reuse what a model learns elsewhere.

The model uses self-supervised pretraining and an atlas-grounded scheme for turning recordings into tokens. The tokenization has no session-specific components, allowing the model to learn globally shared spatiotemporal representations. This design supports a common representation across recordings, rather than requiring a separate session-specific component to organize each one.

Across multiple widefield datasets, WiCAT outperforms baseline models and supports lightweight downstream decoding. The reported transfers span subjects, tasks, and datasets. Particularly significant are continuous behavior decoding without adaptation to unseen subjects and reconstruction of left-out brain regions on those subjects. These results establish a step toward foundation modeling for widefield data, showing that a shared anatomical organization can support representations useful beyond the recordings used for pretraining.
icml-2026-cross-subject-modeling-for-wid.tldr: WiCAT uses atlas-grounded self-supervised representations to transfer widefield calcium-imaging models across subjects and decode behavior on unseen subjects.

paragraphs: dgMARK embeds detectable watermarks in text from discrete diffusion language models by controlling token unmasking order. These models can fill token positions in different sequences. Although an ideal conditional predictor would be unaffected by that ordering, practical models are sensitive to it. The paper uses this sensitivity as a channel through which generation can carry a statistical signature.

The method favors positions whose high-reward candidate tokens meet a parity rule determined by a binary hash. It therefore guides which positions are filled without explicitly reweighting the model’s learned token probabilities. The procedure works with common ordering strategies based on confidence, entropy, or margins, and a one-step lookahead variant can strengthen the watermark.

Detection looks for an unusually high frequency of parity matches in the resulting text. A sliding-window detector provides robustness to editing operations, including insertion, deletion, substitution, and paraphrasing. The contribution connects watermark construction to a distinctive property of diffusion decoding: ordering decisions themselves can shape a detectable signal while fitting into existing decoding strategies.
icml-2026-dgmark-decoding-guided-waterma.tldr: dgMARK watermarks diffusion-generated text by steering token unmasking order toward a detectable hash-based parity pattern.

paragraphs: DLEBench evaluates whether instruction-based image editors can reliably change small objects. Existing benchmarks show strong instruction following and reasoning, but those successes leave precise local editing underexplored. The new benchmark focuses on objects occupying only 1%–10% of an image, making the requested changes concern a small part of the overall scene.

The testbed contains 1,889 samples covering seven instruction types. It includes challenging cases with partial occlusion and edits involving multiple objects. Its evaluation protocol separately considers instruction following and visual consistency, using refined scoring rubrics to reduce ambiguity and subjective interpretation. This distinction helps assess both whether the requested change occurred and whether the edited image remains visually consistent.

The authors also introduce tool-driven and oracle-guided evaluation modes to address disagreement between multimodal model judges and human assessments. Tests on ten image-editing models reveal substantial performance gaps in editing small objects. These results show why dedicated evaluation matters: plausible performance on broader editing tasks does not fully characterize the ability to make accurate changes to fine details.
icml-2026-dlebench-evaluating-small-scal.tldr: DLEBench exposes gaps in small-object image editing through a dedicated testbed and evaluation protocol addressing automated-judge disagreement.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how brain-relevant visual representations can emerge and become refined without labeled training data. It starts from the observation that even randomly initialized, high-dimensional networks can contain representations aligned with the brain. The question is how sensory experience and developmental changes could stabilize and improve such representations.

The proposed deep spiking neural network begins with an overcomplete architecture and combines unsupervised learning with activity-dependent synaptic pruning. Sensory-driven activity organizes the network while weak or redundant connections are selectively removed. This produces progressively more compact and informative representations, linking representation learning to a developmental mechanism motivated by neuroscience.

Without labels, the resulting hierarchy aligns strongly with neural responses across multiple visual areas in mice and macaques, outperforming the reported supervised and unsupervised ANN and SNN baselines. Pruning further improves alignment and robustness in noisy and few-shot recognition settings. The findings provide a computational account of visual refinement in which initially rich representations are shaped through experience and selective connection removal, connecting emergent alignment with biologically grounded learning.
icml-2026-emergent-visual-representation.tldr: An unsupervised spiking network develops brain-aligned visual representations that improve further when weak or redundant synapses are pruned.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether reinforcement learning can be both sample-efficient and replicable when an agent must explore through interaction. Earlier theoretical bounds left a large gap between settings with convenient generative access and episodic settings requiring exploration. That gap raised the possibility that exploration itself might impose a substantial extra cost for replicability.

For low-horizon tabular Markov decision processes, the authors give a replicable algorithm using approximately S squared times A samples, expressed as a soft-O bound. Here, S denotes the number of states and A the number of actions. This substantially improves the previous exploration upper bound and brings generative and episodic learning closer together.

The paper also establishes an episodic lower bound with approximately quadratic dependence on S. That makes the algorithm nearly optimal in its dependence on the state-space size, rather than establishing optimality in every parameter. Within the stated low-horizon tabular setting, the results nearly resolve the central question: requiring exploration need not be a major obstacle to sample-efficient replicable learning.
icml-2026-from-generative-to-episodic-sa.tldr: For low-horizon tabular problems, a new replicable RL algorithm nearly closes the sample-efficiency gap between generative access and episodic exploration.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether making individual expert models better also makes their merged model better. A common workflow fine-tunes a shared foundation model on specialized tasks and then combines the resulting checkpoints. The authors challenge the assumption that improvements achieved during expert training necessarily carry through to the merging stage.

Their experiments show that prolonged fine-tuning aimed at improving experts individually can degrade merged-model performance. This pattern appears in vision and language, at multiple model scales, and for both full fine-tuning and LoRA adaptation. The analysis traces the degradation to a small set of difficult examples that dominate late training and become memorized.

That memorization produces negative interference between parameters, while the associated knowledge is forgotten during merging. Task-dependent, aggressive early stopping substantially improves the reported merging outcomes. The practical implication is that checkpoint selection should account for the intended merged model: the training duration that favors a standalone expert can differ from the duration that preserves useful compatibility among experts.
icml-2026-from-memorization-to-parameter.tldr: Prolonged expert fine-tuning can harm model merging through memorization and parameter interference, while task-dependent early stopping improves merged performance.

paragraphs: Hierarchical Multi-view HAAR addresses graph learning when neighboring nodes often have different labels. In this setting, aggregation can become dominated by highly connected nodes, while spectral filtering can blur signals or introduce approximation errors. The proposed framework organizes information across a graph hierarchy to preserve useful distinctions and handle interactions at multiple scales.

HMH first learns signed affinities informed by node features and graph structure, then uses those embeddings to construct a soft hierarchy. At each level, a sparse, orthonormal Haar basis supports learnable filtering in the frequency domain while retaining locality. Skip connections and unpooling combine the hierarchical outputs back at the original graph resolution.

This construction targets hub domination, oversmoothing, and bottlenecks that compress long-range information. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art spectral baselines of up to 3% for node classification and 7% for graph classification, alongside linear scalability in the evaluations. The framework’s stated near-linear computational scaling makes its multiscale treatment relevant to larger graphs, rather than requiring a costly dense representation of their spectral structure.
icml-2026-hierarchical-multi-scale-graph.tldr: HMH uses a learned graph hierarchy and local Haar spectral filters to improve scalable learning on heterophilous graphs.

paragraphs: Just Y-Prediction addresses learning from datasets whose labels contain errors. Label diffusion models approach classification by modeling class posteriors, but commonly train by predicting Gaussian noise. The paper argues that this prediction target lacks explicit class meaning, limiting optimization and inference when training labels are unreliable.

The proposed JYP paradigm instead predicts labels directly, allowing the model to characterize the label manifold with explicit semantic guidance. The authors prove that, within their label diffusion framework, JYP converges to an optimal solution equivalent to that of noise prediction. They also report accelerated convergence and support for one-step inference, connecting the change in prediction target to practical efficiency.

Building on JYP, the method uses accumulated historical inconsistency to adapt optimization for clean, noisy, and hard examples. This lets training respond differently to samples with different reliability and difficulty. Experiments report consistent improvements over competitors on synthetic noisy datasets and state-of-the-art results on multiple real-world benchmarks. Together, the results support direct label prediction as a foundation for both efficient diffusion classification and more adaptive treatment of unreliable supervision.
icml-2026-just-y-prediction-enabling-his.tldr: JYP trains label diffusion models to predict labels directly, enabling one-step inference and adaptive learning from clean, noisy, and hard samples.

paragraphs: This paper tackles the cost of modeling interatomic interactions for large molecular dynamics simulations. Learning-based message passing methods can become difficult to scale or lose accuracy through overly coarse representations. The proposed framework aims to retain full atomic resolution while using a sparser structure to exchange information among atoms.

Its neural network stacks message-passing layers that follow distinct, dilated star-shaped paths. These paths are constructed progressively across regions to capture interactions that depend on distance. The central design replaces dense interatomic communication with sparse, region-based message-passing graphs, allowing the model to address large systems without abandoning individual-atom detail.

Evaluation covers four benchmarks with substantially different system sizes and structures: MD22 molecules with 42–370 atoms, the 166-atom Chignolin protein, AdK trajectories reaching 3,000 atoms, and MISATO protein–ligand systems reaching 40,000 atoms. The reported results achieve state-of-the-art performance overall across the benchmarks. This range supports the framework’s intended combination of accuracy and scale across molecules, protein conformations, and heterogeneous protein–ligand complexes.
icml-2026-large-scale-molecular-dynamics.tldr: Dilated, region-based message passing models interatomic interactions sparsely while retaining full atomic resolution for large molecular systems.

paragraphs: Finslerian Reinforcement Learning combines direction-dependent movement costs with an objective sensitive to rare, severe outcomes. Its locomotion cost depends on both the current state and the direction of motion. This allows uphill and downhill travel, or motion involving lateral slip, to have different costs even when other aspects of the movement are similar.

FiRL uses Conditional Value-at-Risk to account for adverse outcomes. The authors derive a corresponding risk-sensitive Bellman equation and show that its operator is a contraction, guaranteeing a unique fixed-point value function. They also show that the induced path cost satisfies a triangle inequality despite being directionally asymmetric. An actor–critic algorithm then learns policies under this combined objective.

Simulation benchmarks and real robot trials report safer, more energy-efficient locomotion than strong baselines including risk-neutral PPO. On a 12-degree sloped Hopper task, FiRL reduces worst-case impact forces measured by CVaR at 0.1 by over 35% and total energy cost by 15%, while improving success rate. These results connect the mathematical treatment of directional effort and tail risk to concrete locomotion benefits.
icml-2026-learning-anisotropic-value-geo.tldr: FiRL combines direction-dependent locomotion costs with tail-risk optimization to learn safer, more energy-efficient movement policies.

paragraphs: MASPOB optimizes prompts in multi-agent systems whose workflows cannot be changed. This setting makes prompt improvement valuable but difficult: evaluating a complete system is costly, prompts interact through the workflow, and the number of possible prompt combinations grows rapidly. The method addresses these challenges within a limited evaluation budget.

A bandit framework uses upper confidence bounds to balance testing uncertain candidates against exploiting candidates that already look promising. Graph neural networks incorporate the system’s topology into representations of prompt semantics, helping account for how one agent’s instructions interact with others. Coordinate ascent then decomposes joint optimization into subproblems that vary one coordinate at a time.

The authors describe this decomposition as reducing search complexity from exponential to linear. Across diverse benchmarks, MASPOB achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently outperforms the reported baselines. The approach matters because it treats prompt quality as a property of an interconnected system: budget-aware exploration, structural modeling, and simpler optimization steps jointly support improvement without modifying the workflow itself.
icml-2026-maspob-bandit-based-prompt-opt.tldr: MASPOB combines bandit search, graph representations, and coordinate ascent to optimize interacting agent prompts under a limited evaluation budget.

paragraphs: This paper studies why large diffusion vision-language models become repetitive and less visually grounded during long-form generation. These models offer parallel decoding and bidirectional context, but the authors identify two mechanisms that undermine those advantages as generation proceeds. Both mechanisms arise within the decoding process rather than from a new downstream task.

First, tokens begin as masks, and their hidden representations progressively drift toward a shared mask-prior direction. The paper links this drift to repetition. Second, positional attention bias conflicts with iterative unmasking and suppresses attention to informative visual tokens. That conflict weakens the connection between generated text and the image it should describe.

The proposed remedy combines Mask Prior Suppression with Monotonic RoPE Scaling during decoding. It requires no additional training and can be plugged into existing models. Experiments report improvements on general multimodal evaluations and visual grounding tasks, with robust gains for long descriptions across diverse architectures. The findings show that targeted changes to decoding can address both repetitive output and weakened visual attention in the evaluated models.
icml-2026-mitigating-mask-prior-drift-an.tldr: Two training-free decoding interventions reduce repetition and improve visual grounding in diffusion vision-language models, especially for long descriptions.

paragraphs: NNEinFact makes custom nonnegative tensor factorization easier to specify and fit. Researchers working with multiway data often must choose between a small set of established models, implement a custom method, or use gradient optimization that struggles with nonnegativity constraints. This paper provides a general multiplicative-update procedure for models expressible as tensor contractions.

A researcher specifies the model using an einsum string and chooses from supported loss functions, including the alpha–beta divergence. The algorithm handles missing data and converges to a stationary point of the loss. That convergence claim concerns a stationary solution, rather than a guarantee of the globally best factorization. The reported implementation can fit tensors containing hundreds of millions of entries in seconds.

On real-world prediction tasks, custom models fitted with NNEinFact outperform standard models by over 37%. Compared with gradient-based methods, it achieves less than half the test loss and converges up to 90 times faster in the reported experiments. These findings connect flexible model specification with practical optimization, reducing the implementation burden of tailoring a factorization to particular data.
icml-2026-near-universal-multiplicative-.tldr: NNEinFact fits custom nonnegative tensor contractions from an einsum specification using fast multiplicative updates with stationary-point convergence.

paragraphs: Neural Graph Dispersion addresses the task of generating a collection of structurally different graphs. Given graphs on N unlabeled vertices, a distance measure, and a desired collection size k, the objective is to maximize pairwise diversity. Unlike ordinary generative modeling, this problem supplies no target distribution from which to obtain training examples.

The method makes diversity itself the optimization objective. An ensemble of generators is trained under a repulsive potential that encourages their outputs to spread through graph space according to the chosen distance. Diverse graphs are obtained along the optimization trajectories. This formulation avoids fitting an example distribution and, as stated by the authors, avoids per-metric retraining.

Experiments report high diversity while scaling both graph size N and collection size k an order of magnitude beyond prior work. The contribution is a way to use neural generators for a task defined by separation among outputs rather than resemblance to observed samples. It broadens the role of generative optimization in graph construction, where combinatorial and iterative search have been the predominant approaches.
icml-2026-neural-dispersion-on-graphs-60.tldr: Neural Graph Dispersion directly optimizes an ensemble of graph generators for structural diversity without fitting a target data distribution.

paragraphs: OMatG-IRL adapts continuous-time crystal generators to explicit objectives through reinforcement learning at inference time. Policy-gradient approaches typically require a score that flow-based models do not explicitly learn. These models instead learn velocity fields describing generation dynamics. The proposed framework works directly with those fields, removing the need to compute the score.

The method introduces stochastic perturbations into the generation dynamics to support exploration and policy-gradient estimation while preserving the pretrained generator’s baseline performance. Applied to crystal structure prediction, it reinforces an energy-based objective and uses composition conditioning to preserve diversity. The authors describe this as the first application of reinforcement learning to crystal structure prediction.

Reported performance is competitive with score-based reinforcement-learning approaches. The framework also learns velocity-annealing schedules that vary over generation time, achieving accurate crystal prediction with an order-of-magnitude improvement in sampling efficiency and a corresponding reduction in generation time. These findings show two uses for the same inference-time framework: steering generation toward a physical objective and improving how efficiently the generator reaches its output.
icml-2026-open-materials-generation-with.tldr: OMatG-IRL applies inference-time reinforcement learning directly to crystal generators’ velocity fields, improving objective alignment and sampling efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper explores a model-auditing technique for surfacing hidden information that black-box testing may miss. Called overthinking, it amplifies the parameter changes associated with reasoning distillation. The method requires the weights of a base instruction model and a corresponding reasoning-distilled model, making the intervention a direct modification of model parameters.

The authors subtract the base model’s weights from the reasoning model’s weights, scale that difference by a factor greater than one, and add it back to the base. This extrapolates beyond the reasoning model along the same parameter direction. Layer-wise attenuation strategies selectively control amplification to preserve output quality and coherence.

Across four experimental settings and models ranging from 2B to 32B parameters, amplified models are more likely to reveal hidden information. The findings suggest that secrets or unintended learned behaviors may surface up to ten times more frequently than in the original reasoning model. The mechanism varies by secret type: some disclosures require the reasoning direction, while others occur under any sufficiently large weight perturbation. This distinction qualifies how specifically the effects can be attributed to reasoning amplification.
icml-2026-overthinking-amplifying-reason.tldr: Amplifying reasoning-related weight changes can expose hidden learned information more frequently, with effects that depend on the type of secret.

paragraphs: Plan, Decouple, Assimilate generates remote-sensing training examples by inserting target objects into real backgrounds. This can help address scarce labels and uneven class distributions, but inserted objects must fit their surroundings. The paper targets three failures: inappropriate placement, mismatched illumination or atmospheric appearance, and visible discontinuities in local texture.

The planning module automatically creates geometrically valid bounding boxes. During generation, the decoupling module uses Asymmetric Spectral Adaptation to separate an object’s structural identity from environmental illumination. The assimilation module then uses neighborhood-aware texture processing to harmonize the insertion with its local surroundings. Together, these stages address consistency from overall geometry down to fine texture.

Experiments report a 15.7% reduction in whole-image FID relative to the strongest baseline and an average mAP50 improvement of 17.07 points over using real data. These results connect more consistent synthesis with improved downstream object detection. The approach’s significance is therefore twofold: it improves the visual quality of inserted objects and produces augmented examples that are useful for training detectors in the evaluated remote-sensing settings.
icml-2026-plan-decouple-assimilate-physi.tldr: PDA coordinates placement, illumination, and texture when inserting remote-sensing objects, improving generated-image quality and downstream detection.

paragraphs: TextME expands multimodal representations using text descriptions for projection training. Conventional expansion often needs large paired datasets linking text with images, audio, molecules, or other modalities. Such data can be expensive, especially when annotation requires expertise. The framework instead uses an LLM embedding space as a common destination for diverse pretrained modality representations.

The approach exploits geometric structure already present in pretrained contrastive encoders. The authors empirically identify consistent modality gaps across image, video, audio, 3D, X-ray, and molecular domains. That structure allows projections learned through text alone to support zero-shot transfer across modalities without paired supervision in the expansion training.

Experiments show that text-only projection training preserves substantial performance of the pretrained encoders. The shared space also supports retrieval between modality pairs that were not explicitly aligned during training, including audio-to-image and 3D-to-image retrieval. These findings make text descriptions a practical bridge for modality expansion, with the transfer relying on pretrained encoders and their existing geometry rather than requiring new paired datasets for every connection.
icml-2026-textme-bridging-unseen-modalit.tldr: TextME uses text-only projection training and pretrained encoder geometry to connect modalities in a shared LLM embedding space.

paragraphs: This paper develops theoretical foundations for guiding continuous-time score-based diffusion models in planning tasks. Guidance is used to steer generation toward prescribed constraints, making its accuracy especially relevant when plans have safety requirements. The authors use Doob’s h-transform to characterize an ideal guided diffusion process and provide a reference for analyzing practical guidance.

The analysis examines the discrepancy between that ideal process and approximate guidance. It supplies explicit error bounds and probabilistic guarantees for satisfying prescribed constraints. These guarantees describe constraint satisfaction in probabilistic terms; they do not amount to unconditional certainty that every generated plan satisfies every constraint. The distinction ties safety claims to the analyzed approximation.

The formulation also induces a stochastic optimal control problem, creating a route to practical guidance design without additional model training. Demonstrations cover two-dimensional navigation and joint-trajectory generation for a seven-degree-of-freedom Franka robot. The contribution links an ideal mathematical description, quantifiable approximation error, and implementable planning guidance within one framework, giving the reported applications a theoretical basis for evaluating constraint satisfaction.
icml-2026-training-free-guided-diffusion.tldr: A Doob’s h-transform framework connects training-free diffusion planning guidance with approximation bounds and probabilistic constraint-satisfaction guarantees.

paragraphs: OneTrackerV2 unifies visual object tracking across RGB and multimodal inputs. Existing approaches often require separate models for different modalities or adaptation from pretrained models, increasing the burden of training and deployment. The proposed framework uses shared parameters and a single end-to-end training process to support multiple tracking tasks within one architecture.

A Meta Merger maps multimodal information into a unified space, enabling flexible fusion. The framework then divides expert specialization into two parts. T-MoE models spatial and temporal relationships needed for tracking, while M-MoE represents multimodal knowledge. This separation is designed to disentangle cross-modal dependencies and reduce conflicts among features.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance across five RGB and RGB-plus-additional-modality tracking tasks and twelve benchmarks, while maintaining high inference efficiency. Strong performance persists after model compression, and the tracker is robust when modalities are missing. Together, these findings support sharing a tracking architecture across input configurations while retaining specialized processing for motion relationships and modality information.
icml-2026-unified-multimodal-visual-trac.tldr: OneTrackerV2 combines shared multimodal fusion with separate tracking and modality experts for efficient tracking across input configurations.

paragraphs: This paper treats generation order as a central part of masked diffusion language modeling. Text quality depends strongly on which positions are generated first. Prior approaches either fix that order or learn an ordering policy after pretraining the diffusion model, adding cost and potentially producing suboptimal results through separate optimization stages.

The authors introduce an order-expressive masked diffusion framework covering a broad class of generation processes. It provides a shared interpretation of masked diffusion, autoregressive generation, and block diffusion. Building on that formulation, their learnable-order model trains the ordering mechanism and diffusion backbone together from scratch using one objective.

Joint training lets the model generate text in an order that depends on context, allowing ordering and token generation to be learned as connected decisions. Experiments report that the learnable-order model outperforms various discrete diffusion models across multiple language-modeling benchmarks. The contribution combines a unifying description of generation orders with an empirical case for learning order alongside the generator, rather than committing to it independently.
icml-2026-unifying-masked-diffusion-mode.tldr: LoMDM jointly learns context-dependent generation order and a masked diffusion backbone within a framework spanning several generation styles.
